chapter_theme: The council of the Vidyadhara king: a first counsellor praises a line of lords and women, then Sumantiri speaks, naming Achuvakandan, a youth firm in austerity and the sage's prophecy that he will reach heaven and then liberation, and ends by saying fate may overturn all plans.

cast.role: the first counsellor of the Vidyadhara king, who speaks in 335-346 (unnamed, identity uncertain)
the fourth of the Vidyadhara king's four counsellors, who speaks from 348
king of the Vidyadharas of the southern ridge
the youth, son of Jayasenan of Bhavagiri, firm in austerity
king of Bhavagiri, the youth's father

335.reading: The speaker begins by saying that, among the crowned kings, one has no one to turn aside his rod, and that he will tell the king a little of what now presses on them.
335.nuance: Who 'he' is in lines 1-2 is not fixed by the verse; the sense is left open.
335.event: The first counsellor opens his speech to the king.

336.reading: The speaker names a lord of the golden city of the ridge, Megavahana, who rules it in comfort with his proud rutting elephants and bright spear.
336.nuance: The ridge city is the Vidyadhara realm of the sarukkam before; the verse names the lord and his elephants only.

337.reading: A woman with curling hair like a peacock's tail, hummed over by bees, is named Megamalini.
337.nuance: Her tie to Megavahana is not stated in the verse; a daughter is the likely sense.

338.reading: A man named Vichuvan, of old renown, is said to have come to worship her goddess and to rule happily, even commanding Death.
338.nuance: The verse says he 'came to worship her god' (தெய்வம் வழிபட மேவி வந்தனன்) without saying where; the last line's claim that he commands Death is boast-like praise.

339.reading: The speaker says that one born to rule the sky-world and be a door of rescue for earthly beings has appeared, and the world grows once its griefs have gone.
339.nuance: The person praised is not named; the lines are hard to construe.

340.reading: The same lord, having ruled the sky-world by a boon, came here, gave long grace, and then became a light bright as the moon and fit for the world above.
340.event: He gives grace and then takes his place above.

341.reading: The speaker says that, with the thought of ending others' darkness through himself, he is such a one that no other would think ill of him.

342.reading: If the girl's lover comes to the chest of the garland-wearer, then evening, moon and daylight all seem to meet in one.
342.nuance: The lines are in the style of lovers' praise; the exact comparison is hard to fix.

343.reading: The sister of the lord is praised as a wishing-tree branch with fragrant hair and carp-long eyes.

344.reading: A woman wearing bright jewels, whose hair is hummed over by kinnara bees, is named Jothimalai.

345.reading: A lord whose name joins the sun's is set beside a long-eyed woman whose breast is likened to the whole earth.
345.nuance: Lines 2-4 are hard to construe; the lord's name is not spelled out.

346.reading: The speaker ends by asking the king, if grace is in him, to weigh what he has said and act on it.
346.event: The first counsellor closes his advice and asks the king to act.

347.reading: The poet says that the garland-wearer, having heard all this and understood the intent, spoke calming words to the first speaker, and Sumantiri, the fourth of the girl's father's four companions, began to speak.
347.nuance: Whose heart 'the garland-wearer' is understood to read is not quite clear from the lines.
347.event: The first counsellor finishes, and Sumantiri, the fourth counsellor, takes up the counsel.

348.reading: Sumantiri says it is not right to weigh the claim of the elder Achuvakandan, whose order none can turn aside, nor to give the maiden to spear-bearers, and that she stay unwed is no honour.
348.nuance: The chain of reasons in lines 1-4 is hard to follow; whether he refuses or urges Achuvakandan's claim is uncertain.
348.event: Sumantiri begins by naming Achuvakandan and the maiden's unwed state.

349.reading: Sumantiri says that for the son, bright as the sun-god, of the golden-eared ruler of the walled city of Surendra, ruling the hill-realm by right would be a hard thing.
349.nuance: The ruler and the son are unnamed; it is unclear which side the verse favours.

350.reading: Though the sword-like glances of women, dark-lined and flickering like carp, strike at him as weapons, the young man keeps a steady mind and stands high in austerity.
350.nuance: The youth is not named until verse 353; verses 350-353 are read as describing Vijayapathiran. The weapons are the women's eyes, read as a figure.

claims.claim: a youth firm in austerity is not shaken by women's glances

351.reading: The youth does not take to the beat of drums, the songs and dances of women, and turns from heavenly pleasures, a handsome man like one of the gods.
351.nuance: The Jain frame is inferred from the later naming of the sage Asodharan; the verse itself only describes the youth's distaste.

claims.claim: turning away from sensual pleasure marks one fit for release

352.reading: His father, in a festival at the shrine of the sage of Chitrakuta, bows to the avadhi-knower named Yasodhara and asks about his son's future.
352.nuance: The father is named Jayasenan only in verse 353.
352.event: The father goes to Asodharan at Chitrakuta and asks about his son.

353.reading: Sumantiri names the youth: Vijayapathiran, son of Jayasenan, king of Bhavagiri, and his queen Pritimati.

354.reading: The youth will give up the rule that protects the world, practise austerity, reach Indra's world Sasara, and rule there as lord of the gods for seventeen oceans of time.
354.nuance: The lines are the sage's prophecy as Sumantiri reports it; the later 'we heard' (355) shows it is reported speech.
354.event: The sage foretells the youth's rebirth as a god.

claims.claim: a king who gives up rule for austerity gains the lordship of the gods

355.reading: So, Sumantiri says, having enjoyed divine pleasures he will not be dazzled into taking kings' wealth for substance, and will reach Sivagati by austerity that ends all evil: this was the sage's word.
355.nuance: Sivagati here is the Jain word for liberation; it need not mean Siva's grace.
355.event: Sumantiri closes his report of the sage's words.

claims.claim: austerity ends all evil and brings one to liberation
kings' wealth is not a real thing to rely on

356.reading: Sumantiri says that through austerity, wide knowledge and the body's nature of leaving in this life, the thoughtful reach the place of the god, and truly have no need of kin of karma.
356.nuance: கருமச் சுற்றம் is read as kin bound by deed or duty; the sense turns on that phrase.

claims.claim: austerity and clear knowledge, with the body's passing, lead the mind to the divine seat

357.reading: Sumantiri says that even if a swayamvara were proclaimed with drums and conches and crowds, they cannot tell whether they dare face Achuvakandan, king, for that is a matter for the brave.
357.nuance: Lines 2-3 are hard; the swayamvara is read as a conditional.

358.reading: Sumantiri says that when they plan one thing, fate decides the result, and a plan pressed hard may end otherwise, so none can say the course is certain; if they decide today he will say a little more.
358.nuance: The fate claim is used as a counsellor's caution, not as a reason to give up counsel; he still offers to speak further.
358.event: Sumantiri warns that fate may overturn their plans and offers more counsel.

claims.claim: fate decides the outcome of human planning, and plans may end otherwise than intended

links.note: Verse 11 says the perfumes and flowers of the land are so heavy that even ascetics in good austerity are weakened; verse 350 shows a youth who stands high in austerity while women's glances strike him.
links.teaches: The poem first lets the land's pleasures unseat ascetics, then offers a youth who stays firm, so the earlier fall is shown as common and not necessary.

links.note: Naladiyar 11 says that the wise renounce in childhood because they know grey hair will come; verse 351 shows a youth who turns from music, dance and heaven-like pleasure while still young.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar gives the reason for early renunciation and the epic gives a young man living it, so the reader sees how the reason looks as a character.

gains.a: A reason for the youth's distaste, the argument from coming old age, which the verse never gives.
gains.b: A named young man who has already done what the quatrain says the wise do.

links.note: Tirumanthiram 634 says those who do austerity become lords of Amaravati and live in bliss by the Lord's grace; verse 354 says a king who leaves his rule for austerity becomes lord of the gods, with no god named as the giver.
links.teaches: The same heavenly kingship is credited to the ascetic's own austerity by the Jain sage and to the Lord's grace by Tirumular, so the two disagree about who gives the reward.

gains.a: A giver of the reward, which the sage's prophecy leaves out, against which the claim of earned rule can be measured.
gains.b: A path to the same heaven that needs no grace, which tests the claim that grace gives it.

links.note: Tirumanthiram 258 names austerity and virtue as a boat across the sea of deeds that the Lord makes fruitful; verse 355 says austerity ends all evil and reaches Sivagati, with the god unnamed.
links.teaches: Both name austerity as what ends deeds, but one adds a god who makes it bear fruit and the other leaves effort alone to do it, so the dispute is over what austerity needs.

gains.a: A second agent, the Lord, against which to weigh the sage's claim that effort alone ends evil.
gains.b: A case where austerity is said to bring release with no god named, which tests how far it depends on grace.

links.note: Naladiyar 27 praises the firm who see the body as a bubble and resolve to end their wandering; verse 356 says the body's nature of leaving, with austerity and knowledge, brings the mind to the divine seat.
links.teaches: The quatrain stops at the resolve born of seeing the body pass, and the epic names where that resolve is said to lead.

gains.a: A reason that the body's passing matters: it is the ground of the resolve that leads to the divine seat.
gains.b: A destination for the firm resolve, which the quatrain leaves at the ending of birth.

links.note: Kural 380 says that nothing is stronger than fate, which arrives first even when one devises another way; verse 358 says that when they plan, fate gives the result and a strong plan may end otherwise, and Sumantiri still goes on to counsel.
links.teaches: The couplet gives fate as a rule; the minister uses it as a caution that does not stop deliberation, so the rule is shown as bounding counsel and not replacing it.

gains.a: A use of the fate rule as a counsellor's caution, which the couplet's flat statement does not show.
gains.b: A scene of deliberation where the rule is applied, so its strength is tested against a council that goes on planning.

links.note: Civaka Cintamani 215 makes a king heedless of a warning because an earlier-formed destiny rose in him; verse 358 has a counsellor name fate as the power over plans and still press counsel.
links.teaches: One epic makes fate the reason a king ignores counsel and the other makes it the reason counsel must be given with humility, so fate is shown as excusing the king in one and humbling the adviser in the other.

source_issues: Verses 335-346: the identity of the speaker, of the persons named (Megavahana, Megamalini, Vichuvan, Jothimalai) and their ties to one another are not fixed by the verses; many lines are hard to construe, so most are flagged uncertain.
Verse 344 line 1 and 345 line 2: the word division makes the sense doubtful.
Verses 348-349 and 357: the argument about Achuvakandan and the maiden's hand is not clear from the Tamil alone.
